title: Financial security: protecting your money from fraud
subtitle: Financial security
openingQuestion: You get a video call from someone whose face and voice are identical to your company's 'boss,' asking you to urgently transfer 500 million VND to a 'partner' for an emergency reason, right during work hours. What kind of scam could this be, one that's on the rise recently?
openingOptions: This is certainly a completely real call, since video call technology today can't possibly be faked
A deepfake scam - AI faking the voice and face of someone you know
Just checking the caller ID number shown on screen is enough to confirm this is a real call
There's nothing to worry about at all, since video calls always accurately verify the caller's true identity
explanation: Deepfake is AI technology that can generate fake images and voices identical to a real person, increasingly exploited by scammers to impersonate company executives, relatives, and even police/bank staff to demand an urgent money transfer from the victim. The common trait of this kind of scam is creating a sense of URGENCY and TIME PRESSURE so the victim doesn't have time to think or verify through another channel. The safety principle: always verify through an independent communication channel (call the person's known number directly, message them through a different app) before transferring any large amount, no matter how familiar the requester seems.

realWorldExample.company: Warnings from the State Bank of Vietnam and the Ministry of Public Security
realWorldExample.description: The State Bank of Vietnam and the Ministry of Public Security have repeatedly issued warnings about common financial scams in Vietnam: impersonating police/prosecutors demanding a transfer for 'verification,' multi-level investment scams promising abnormally high returns (20-50%/month), bank OTP scams (posing as a bank employee calling to ask for an OTP code to 'help resolve an issue'), and, more recently, deepfake scams faking the image/voice of a relative or company executive to trick victims into transferring money.

quiz.question: What's the most easily recognized common trait of most financial scams?
options: They always target elderly people who rarely use a phone
They always ask the victim to transfer through a major bank
They always present a notarized contract to build trust
They create a sense of urgency, leaving no time to verify
quiz.explanation: Scammers typically manufacture a fake emergency (an account frozen, a relative in an accident, an investment opportunity about to expire) so the victim acts hastily, skipping careful verification.

quiz.question: Why should you NEVER give out a bank OTP code over the phone, even if the caller claims to be a bank employee?
options: Because a real bank never asks for an OTP code over the phone
Because the OTP should only be read out when the employee calls from the official hotline number
Because an OTP is single-use, so reading it out is harmless anyway
Because reading out the OTP will freeze the account for 24 hours
quiz.explanation: The OTP code is the final security layer confirming that the actual account holder is making the transaction. A real bank employee doesn't need it and never asks for it - anyone who asks is a clear sign of a scam.

quiz.question: When you receive an investment offer promising 30-50%/month, stable and risk-free, what's the most sensible reaction?
options: Ask for a contract guaranteeing the return before putting in money
Stay highly alert - this is almost always a sign of fraud
Accept it if the offering party has a valid business license
Invest a small amount first to test whether the promise is real
quiz.explanation: No legitimate investment channel (not even the best-performing growth stock) can guarantee a high, stable, risk-free return over a long period - this is a classic sign of a Ponzi scheme, paying earlier investors with later investors' money, and it collapses once new money stops coming in.

quiz.question: You get a video call from a relative, with the exact face and voice, asking for an urgent transfer of 50 million. What's the safest way to handle it?
options: Ask a few private questions right in that same call and decide whether to transfer
Transfer half the amount first to test it, then verify before sending the rest
Call back using a number saved beforehand, or ask a third party to verify
Ask the caller to record another video confirming it before transferring the money
quiz.explanation: Deepfake can render both face and voice in real time, so any verification done inside that same call could also be faked. The reliable method is switching to a channel the impersonator doesn't control: calling back a number you already saved, or asking a third party.

quiz.question: Why does enabling two-factor authentication on a personal email matter for bank account safety?
options: Because two-factor authentication automatically changes your email password every month
Because banks require email to have two-factor authentication before opening an account
Because every money transfer requires a confirmation code sent to your inbox
Because email is usually the password-recovery point for every other financial account
quiz.explanation: Taking over an email is taking over a master key: the attacker uses 'forgot password' to take over other accounts one by one. Protecting this root layer is usually worth more than setting a complex password on each separate service.

keyTakeaways: AI deepfakes faking image/voice are a rising new form of scam - always verify through an independent channel before transferring money for an urgent request
Never give a bank OTP code to anyone over the phone, even someone claiming to be a bank employee
Abnormally high, stable, risk-free returns are a warning sign of a multi-level/Ponzi scheme
The general rule: slow down, verify through another channel, don't act under time pressure when money is involved

practicePrompt.question: You get a message from a 'bank' saying your account shows unusual activity, with a link to 'verify your identity' and a request to enter the OTP code you just received. What should you do?
options: Don't give out the OTP through any channel, and call the official hotline yourself to verify
Enter the OTP code right away into the link included in the message to verify your identity quickly as requested
Call back the exact number that sent the message to ask for more details before giving them the OTP
Ignore this message entirely, with no further verification needed, since your bank account is always absolutely safe
practicePrompt.explanation: The general rule: don't act under time pressure, always verify through an independent channel (an official hotline you already know) instead of trusting a link or phone number in a suspicious message.

summary.commonMistake: Reading the concept as a phrase to memorize rather than a principle to apply to a real decision.

application.title: Review right now
application.message: Check whether anyone has recently messaged or called urging you to transfer money urgently - if so, try contacting that person again through a different channel to verify.
application.secondary: A 2-minute verification call can save you a large sum of money.

sections.text: A portfolio carefully built over many years can be wiped out in just a few minutes if it falls into a financial scam trap. Financial security, therefore, matters no less than picking stocks or allocating assets.

Financial fraud in Vietnam is growing more sophisticated, no longer limited to the crude fake prize-winning texts of before. AI technology, especially deepfakes, is being exploited to create far harder-to-detect scam scenarios, while multi-level investment schemes keep reappearing under new names (crypto, forex, 'super-profit' real estate).
Three common types of fraud to recognize

items: Multi-level/Ponzi investment fraud: promises abnormally high, stable returns, encourages recruiting more participants for a commission - collapses when new inflows dry up
Deepfake fraud: uses AI to fake the image or voice of someone you know or a company executive via video call or recording to demand an urgent transfer
OTP code fraud/bank impersonation: calls claiming to be a bank employee or police officer, asking for an OTP code or account information to 'resolve an issue' or 'verify identity'
Fake stock exchange/crypto platforms: sets up a website or app that looks identical to a real exchange, displaying fake profits on the interface to lure victims into depositing more money

sections.label: The 'stop - verify - act' rule
sections.text: When you receive any urgent transfer request (whether from a 'boss,' a 'relative,' a 'bank,' or 'police'), STOP first, don't react immediately. Next, VERIFY through an independent communication channel - call the person's known number directly (not a number from the message/call you just received), or ask through a different chat channel. Only ACT once you've verified for certain. A few minutes delayed to verify is never 'too late' if the request is real.
Protecting personal information - the first line of defense

Many scams begin because the fraudster already has the victim's personal information (full name, ID number, a relative's phone number, even a voice sample from earlier calls) - making the scam scenario far more convincing. Limiting how much personal and financial information you share on social media, being cautious with online surveys/games that ask for sensitive information, and enabling two-factor authentication (2FA) on every bank account and e-wallet are basic but effective defensive steps.

lines: Financial scammers always rely on haste and credulity - slowing down a few minutes to verify is the cheapest and most effective defense there is.
Financial security isn't paranoia - it's the discipline needed to protect the results of years of saving and investing.
